title: Minimax’s M3.1 Flash Cuts Prices Critical PHP bug found by AI affects majority of web sites
excerpt: Mercury 3, diffusion-based alternative to Claude Haiku. d1-ultra, a highly accurate decision model. Using OpenAI’s models to rewrite and repair...
content:
Minimax M3.1 Flash soon to be open weights

MiniMax released M3.1 Flash, a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 428B total parameters, about 23B active, and a 1,000,000-token context window. Via API, it costs $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, with no long-context surcharge. Weights are due to be released October 23 under a license MiniMax has not disclosed. Reasoning is always on across five effort levels (Low through Max), and requests that try to disable it, such as thinking.type=disabled or effort=none, now return an error; reasoning arrives in a separate reasoning_content field instead of inline <think> tags. For developers on M3, the practical changes are half the per-token price and a reasoning-parsing update, while self-hosting hardware requirements stay unknown until the weights ship. ( MarkTechPost )

GPT-5.6 Sol finds critical security flaw in web language PHP

PHP’s maintainers rushed out a fix on Wednesday for PHP2Shell, a memory-management flaw in software that runs up to 70% of websites; the foundation’s security engineer calls it the project’s worst issue in over a decade and compares it to Heartbleed. Researcher Ryan Austin at the security firm Calif found it in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, during an OpenAI-funded audit, after the problem had sat largely ignored for years because it was considered too hard to exploit. Researchers and engineers, joined by Google’s Wiz team and OpenAI’s own researchers, worked in secret on a fix touching nearly 200 files, but a leak on Hacker News forced them to release it a day ahead of the planned October 22 date. Defenders now fear that AI tools can turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours, and some site operators are taking their sites offline as a precaution. For AI developers, the story shows how their models are now central to security on both sides: the same capabilities that uncover deep bugs can speed up attacks, labs are increasingly expected to fund and coordinate audits of open-source projects that are flooded with AI-found bugs, and the window between a patch’s release and its exploitation is shrinking fast. ( The Wall Street Journal )

Mercury 3, a diffusion-based text model to rival Claude Haiku 5.5

Inception released Mercury 3, a language model that generates text by diffusion rather than one token at a time, and says it matches Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna on quality. Mercury 3 refines many tokens in parallel, which Inception says yields about 1,000 tokens per second, 4x to 8x faster than Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, and GLM-5.3 Flash, with better scores on agentic benchmarks. Launch pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens, matching those two models, and $0.35 per million output tokens, 35 percent below them; that is 50 percent off Inception’s eventual standard price, and the company has not said how long the promotion lasts. Inception has not disclosed the model’s parameter count, and the speed and benchmark results are the company’s own. For developers building latency-sensitive features such as real-time agents, Mercury 3 is an alternative to test against small autoregressive models. ( The DeepView )

Liquid AI’s decision model outperforms Jev on benchmarks

Liquid AI released d1-ultra, a hosted decision model that takes text, images, or both and returns a probability for each possible answer in one forward pass, with no output tokens generated. Questions come in three types: yes/no, pick-one-label, and a score on an ordered rubric. Billing covers input tokens only at $0.042 per million, the same rate as TypeSafe’s Jev, and images cost 1.5 tokens per 32x32-pixel patch. Each question is billed as its own prompt, so three questions on one image bill that image three times, and requests are capped at eight images and 4.5 MB. Liquid reports a score of 65 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, ahead of Jev 1.13 at 58 on the index’s October 13 listing. Parameter count, context length, and per-benchmark results are not public, and weights are not available. For routing, moderation, and triage calls, decision models like d1-ultra offer a fast, affordable alternative to LLMs. ( MarkTechPost )

Putting GPT-6 models to work to repair and rebuild legacy code

OpenAI published results from two new evaluations of how its models handle low-resource programming languages, meaning languages with little public code and documentation to learn from, such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. On MultiLangBench, which asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in each of 20 languages, OpenAI reports that GPT-6 Astra averages an 87.4% test pass rate, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with COBOL rising from 10.9% to 72.1%. The cheaper GPT-6 Luna reaches 40.3% at an estimated $0.77 per sample versus $3.48 for GPT-5.6 Sol. On a separate COBOL-to-C++/Java/Kotlin/Python/Rust migration test requiring byte-for-byte output parity on hidden tests, GPT-6.1 Sol scores 86.6% at low reasoning effort (GPT-5.6 Sol: 5.4%) and 97.9% at higher effort; the migration evaluation is not released, while the MultiLangBench setup and test suite are on GitHub. OpenAI says production migrations still need expert review and testing against business rules. Teams with COBOL or Fortran code can now test these models on their own repositories, and the public MultiLangBench harness lets them check the per-language numbers before relying on them. ( OpenAI )

IBM and partners release llm-d, a Swiss army knife for open AI

The llm-d project, led by Red Hat, IBM, and Google, released version 1.0 of its Kubernetes-native framework for serving large models across multiple accelerators and clouds. It runs on top of inference engines such as vLLM or SGLang and adds distributed routing, a stable API, flow control that prioritizes requests among competing tenants, and upgrades that do not interrupt service. It builds on five existing techniques: prefix-cache-aware routing, KV-cache offloading, batch inference optimization, prefill/decode disaggregation, and wide expert parallelism for mixture-of-experts models. The maintainers report that on an agentic coding workload the prefix-aware router captured 97 percent of available cache reuse, and that IBM and Red Hat ran 3,000 software-engineering agents on a self-hosted deployment for 5 to 10 times less than the price of the same open model as a hosted service; the article gives no test configurations. For teams running open weight models on their own clusters, 1.0 offers a stable API and priority controls that could replace custom routing and scheduling layers, though the cost figures are the project’s own and unverified. ( IBM )

Want to know more about what matters in AI right now?

Read the latest issue of The Batch for in-depth analysis of news and research.

Last week, Andrew talked about the significant difference in AI performance between verifiable tasks, which have clear right answers, and judgement tasks, which require contextual decision-making. AI can also make faster progress on performing verifiable tasks due to powerful training techniques like reinforcement learning. “Society also has a long history of looking at AI’s performance on a subset of tasks and overgeneralizing its capabilities. We saw this when AI beat the human world chess champion (Deep Blue), won Jeopardy (Watson), and excelled at Go (AlphaGo). Each of these moments led to hopes about AI’s immediate applicability to other tasks that turned out to be over-optimistic.”

title: Muse Spark Open leads U.S. open models Reflection releases weights for Beam, a much-anticipated model
excerpt: Grok Voice 3.0 leads voice-to-voice benchmarks. Nvidia 3.5 Super VL is faster, more capable than Lightning. DeepSeek-V-4.1-Flash pushes strong...
content:
Muse Spark Open is one of the top open models in the world

Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 42B parameters per token, with a 1M-token context window and text, image, video and audio input. Meta says it is the most capable US open-weight model, and Artificial Analysis’ independent benchmarks back that up, giving it a 39 on its Intelligence Index. In Meta’s own comparison table it leads on MCP-Atlas (89.2) and JobBench (61.8) but scores 76.4 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, behind Kimi K3 (85.0), GLM 5.3 (83.9) and Qwen3.8 (82.0). The Muse Model License permits fine-tuning, distillation and redistribution, requires products to display “Built with Muse Spark Open,” and requires hosting providers above $20M in 12-month revenue to sign a separate agreement. OpenRouter lists its price at $1.25 per 1M input tokens and $4.25 per 1M output tokens. For developers building tool-calling agents, this is a self-hostable option that scores highest on MCP-Atlas in Meta’s comparison, but it trails the top China-based open models on coding and overall index scores. ( MarkTechPost )

Reflection’s Beam is one of the top open models from the U.S.

Reflection released Beam, its first model, an open weights, text-only model with 501 billion total parameters, 23 billion active, and a 1 million token context window. Artificial Analysis, the benchmarking firm that published the results, gives it a 30 on its Intelligence Index, second among U.S.-based open weights models behind Meta’s Muse Spark Open (39) and tenth among all open weights models. It uses about 26,000 output tokens per task, half of K2 Horizon’s roughly 52,000, and scores 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA but only 3.0% on Terminal-Bench 4.0. On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% of questions correctly but hallucinates on 47%, against 26% for K2 Horizon, and in Reflection’s Mirror CLI harness it scores 28 on the Coding Agent Index, well behind the leaders at 68. For developers choosing a U.S.-origin open weights model, Beam is a token-efficient option for agentic tasks, but its weak terminal results and high hallucination rate argue for testing it on your own workload first. ( Artificial Analysis )

Grok Voice 3.0 tops independent tests of voice models

SpaceXAI released Grok Voice 3.0, a hosted speech-to-speech model that ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (83.2) and Gemini 3.8 Live (82.6). It is served as grok-voice-3.0 on the same /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint at $0.08 per minute, both unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0, and the grok-voice-latest alias already points to it. The API is compatible with OpenAI’s Realtime API, supports 28 voices, SIP for phone calls, and tools including web search, remote MCP servers, and custom functions, with reasoning on by default. The first-place score is not a sweep: on the τ-Voice agentic benchmark it scores 71.6% against GPT-Live-1’s 74.5%, and Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 seconds to first audio, slower than Grok Voice 2.0’s 0.70. Because the endpoint, events, and price carry over, teams on the alias were upgraded automatically, so anyone who needs stable behavior should pin grok-voice-3.0 now, since Grok Voice 2.0 is deprecated. ( MarkTechPost )

Nvidia’s vision-language model is the fastest on the planet

Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120 billion parameter vision-language model for enterprise agents, along with two edge models, Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB (available now) and Bolt E4B 4GB (due Oct. 23). Nvidia says Super VL matches its largest reasoning model on multimodal agentic tasks at about one-fifth the parameter count, and reports up to five times the throughput of comparable models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; on Artificial Analysis’s indepdendent benchmark tests, it leads all available models on tokens/second. Bolt 74B-A9B uses native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory, runs on RTX and DGX Spark hardware, and ships with llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth and vLLM support; NVIDIA ranks it first among open models in its class on PinchBench and second on BrowseComp. Super VL ships with open weights, datasets and training recipes, can be fine-tuned through Nvidia NeMo, and is available on Hugging Face, OpenRouter, ModelScope and as an Nvidia NIM microservice. For developers, Bolt 74B-A9B is a self-hostable agent model that fits on a single 24GB consumer GPU, and the open Super VL weights allow fine-tuning on private data.( Nvidia )

DeepSeek’s Flash model gets a performance update

DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017, an update to its smallest V4.1 model that its Hugging Face model card says reduces task execution time and output length (the company itself gives no figures). In its own testing, the model resolved 77% of tasks on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering benchmark, up from 74.2% for the September version and above the 74% DeepSeek lists for Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5; Opus 5 still leads on seven of the 11 benchmarks DeepSeek published. The update is available now in DeepSeek’s apps and through the existing API model ID at unchanged prices, with weights on Hugging Face under the MIT license. DeepSeek also opened its search engine through a Search API returning up to 50 ranked results per query and added a Fetch API that converts a web page to Markdown, both at 75 cents per 1,000 successful requests and free through Nov. 1 when called via DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code or Codex. Developers using deepseek-flash get the update without code changes, but the speed claim is unquantified and the benchmark numbers are DeepSeek’s own, so latency and output length are worth measuring on real workloads, especially after the nearly five-hour API outage on Oct. 15. ( Silicon Angle )

Meta changes terms of service, won’t claim right to scrape websites

Meta removed a passage from its commercial terms page after critics said it let the company use content from websites tied to business accounts to train its AI. The passage said Meta could use content from such domains, pages, or URLs to “provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain” its products and services. Nieman Lab and Cornell law professor James Grimmelmann read it as a way to train on scraped content for free and override a site’s robots.txt file, which tells crawlers what they may fetch. Meta first said nothing about its crawler use had changed, then deleted the language. Spokesperson Daniel Roberts said the terms applied only to ads and business products, that site owners can still use robots.txt, and that the update gives Meta no new rights over those preferences. Meta has not said what its crawlers do with data collected under the business-product terms, so site owners who want to keep content out of AI training still have only robots.txt to rely on, which compliant crawlers honor voluntarily. ( The Verge )

Want to know more about what matters in AI right now?

Read the latest issue of The Batch for in-depth analysis of news and research.

Last week, Andrew talked about the significant difference in AI performance between verifiable tasks, which have clear right answers, and judgement tasks, which require contextual decision-making. AI can also make faster progress on performing verifiable tasks due to powerful training techniques like reinforcement learning. “One interesting challenge for AI Engineers is that, as verifiable tasks get automated, the need for humans to do judgement tasks — which often requires drawing context from a bewilderingly large array of raw data and identifying the pieces that critically influence a decision — remains important. As I’ve written before, I expect people to continue to have a context advantage over LLMs on many tasks for a long time.”

paragraphs: Muse Spark Open is one of the top open models in the world

Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 42B parameters per token, with a 1M-token context window and text, image, video and audio input. Meta says it is the most capable US open-weight model, and Artificial Analysis’ independent benchmarks back that up, giving it a 39 on its Intelligence Index. In Meta’s own comparison table it leads on MCP-Atlas (89.2) and JobBench (61.8) but scores 76.4 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, behind Kimi K3 (85.0), GLM 5.3 (83.9) and Qwen3.8 (82.0). The Muse Model License permits fine-tuning, distillation and redistribution, requires products to display “Built with Muse Spark Open,” and requires hosting providers above $20M in 12-month revenue to sign a separate agreement. OpenRouter lists its price at $1.25 per 1M input tokens and $4.25 per 1M output tokens. For developers building tool-calling agents, this is a self-hostable option that scores highest on MCP-Atlas in Meta’s comparison, but it trails the top China-based open models on coding and overall index scores. ( MarkTechPost )
Reflection’s Beam is one of the top open models from the U.S.

Reflection released Beam, its first model, an open weights, text-only model with 501 billion total parameters, 23 billion active, and a 1 million token context window. Artificial Analysis, the benchmarking firm that published the results, gives it a 30 on its Intelligence Index, second among U.S.-based open weights models behind Meta’s Muse Spark Open (39) and tenth among all open weights models. It uses about 26,000 output tokens per task, half of K2 Horizon’s roughly 52,000, and scores 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA but only 3.0% on Terminal-Bench 4.0. On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% of questions correctly but hallucinates on 47%, against 26% for K2 Horizon, and in Reflection’s Mirror CLI harness it scores 28 on the Coding Agent Index, well behind the leaders at 68. For developers choosing a U.S.-origin open weights model, Beam is a token-efficient option for agentic tasks, but its weak terminal results and high hallucination rate argue for testing it on your own workload first. ( Artificial Analysis )
Grok Voice 3.0 tops independent tests of voice models

SpaceXAI released Grok Voice 3.0, a hosted speech-to-speech model that ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (83.2) and Gemini 3.8 Live (82.6). It is served as grok-voice-3.0 on the same /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint at $0.08 per minute, both unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0, and the grok-voice-latest alias already points to it. The API is compatible with OpenAI’s Realtime API, supports 28 voices, SIP for phone calls, and tools including web search, remote MCP servers, and custom functions, with reasoning on by default. The first-place score is not a sweep: on the τ-Voice agentic benchmark it scores 71.6% against GPT-Live-1’s 74.5%, and Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 seconds to first audio, slower than Grok Voice 2.0’s 0.70. Because the endpoint, events, and price carry over, teams on the alias were upgraded automatically, so anyone who needs stable behavior should pin grok-voice-3.0 now, since Grok Voice 2.0 is deprecated. ( MarkTechPost )
Nvidia’s vision-language model is the fastest on the planet

Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120 billion parameter vision-language model for enterprise agents, along with two edge models, Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB (available now) and Bolt E4B 4GB (due Oct. 23). Nvidia says Super VL matches its largest reasoning model on multimodal agentic tasks at about one-fifth the parameter count, and reports up to five times the throughput of comparable models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; on Artificial Analysis’s indepdendent benchmark tests, it leads all available models on tokens/second. Bolt 74B-A9B uses native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory, runs on RTX and DGX Spark hardware, and ships with llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth and vLLM support; NVIDIA ranks it first among open models in its class on PinchBench and second on BrowseComp. Super VL ships with open weights, datasets and training recipes, can be fine-tuned through Nvidia NeMo, and is available on Hugging Face, OpenRouter, ModelScope and as an Nvidia NIM microservice. For developers, Bolt 74B-A9B is a self-hostable agent model that fits on a single 24GB consumer GPU, and the open Super VL weights allow fine-tuning on private data.( Nvidia )
DeepSeek’s Flash model gets a performance update

DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017, an update to its smallest V4.1 model that its Hugging Face model card says reduces task execution time and output length (the company itself gives no figures). In its own testing, the model resolved 77% of tasks on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering benchmark, up from 74.2% for the September version and above the 74% DeepSeek lists for Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5; Opus 5 still leads on seven of the 11 benchmarks DeepSeek published. The update is available now in DeepSeek’s apps and through the existing API model ID at unchanged prices, with weights on Hugging Face under the MIT license. DeepSeek also opened its search engine through a Search API returning up to 50 ranked results per query and added a Fetch API that converts a web page to Markdown, both at 75 cents per 1,000 successful requests and free through Nov. 1 when called via DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code or Codex. Developers using deepseek-flash get the update without code changes, but the speed claim is unquantified and the benchmark numbers are DeepSeek’s own, so latency and output length are worth measuring on real workloads, especially after the nearly five-hour API outage on Oct. 15. ( Silicon Angle )
Meta changes terms of service, won’t claim right to scrape websites

Meta removed a passage from its commercial terms page after critics said it let the company use content from websites tied to business accounts to train its AI. The passage said Meta could use content from such domains, pages, or URLs to “provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain” its products and services. Nieman Lab and Cornell law professor James Grimmelmann read it as a way to train on scraped content for free and override a site’s robots.txt file, which tells crawlers what they may fetch. Meta first said nothing about its crawler use had changed, then deleted the language. Spokesperson Daniel Roberts said the terms applied only to ads and business products, that site owners can still use robots.txt, and that the update gives Meta no new rights over those preferences. Meta has not said what its crawlers do with data collected under the business-product terms, so site owners who want to keep content out of AI training still have only robots.txt to rely on, which compliant crawlers honor voluntarily. ( The Verge )

Last week, Andrew talked about the significant difference in AI performance between verifiable tasks, which have clear right answers, and judgement tasks, which require contextual decision-making. AI can also make faster progress on performing verifiable tasks due to powerful training techniques like reinforcement learning. “One interesting challenge for AI Engineers is that, as verifiable tasks get automated, the need for humans to do judgement tasks — which often requires drawing context from a bewilderingly large array of raw data and identifying the pieces that critically influence a decision — remains important. As I’ve written before, I expect people to continue to have a context advantage over LLMs on many tasks for a long time.”

title: Data Mixing, Minus the Guesswork Research from the team behind CausalMix offers a technique to select fine-tuning examples
excerpt: When you’re building a fine-tuning dataset, finding a mix of subject domains that yields a high-performing model can require expensive trial...
content:
What's new: Researchers at Tsinghua University, Ant Group, and Renmin University of China, with Zinan Tang and Yukun Zhang as lead authors, built CausalMix , a method for choosing the share of training examples drawn from various domains regardless of their quality.

Key insight: Datasets can be analyzed according to their data mixture (the proportions of examples that represent different domains) and data quality (variations among examples in difficulty, reasoning complexity, and/or composition). Data mixture and data quality correlate, and finding their correlation in any given dataset makes it possible to differentiate their separate impacts on the performance of a model trained on the dataset. Given a dataset and a consistent training budget, to find the marginal gain of its data mixture — that is, its effect on a fine-tuned model’s performance — we can subtract the effect of data quality from the model’s performance overall. The best data mixture is the one that yields the largest marginal gain.

How it works: The authors compiled 512 subsets of 100,000 examples each drawn from the Tulu 3 dataset. Each subset contained examples for instruction following, coding, math, knowledge, and safety in different proportions. In addition, the authors measured data quality with respect to difficulty, reasoning complexity, and writing clarity as computed by OpenDataArena-Tool . They fine-tuned a separate Qwen2.5-0.5B model on each subset and recorded each fine-tuned model’s performance on 10 benchmarks. Then they trained three models, all of them ensembles of decision trees: one to estimate the portion of each Qwen2.5-0.5B’s performance attributable to data quality, one to estimate the portion of a data mixture that correlates with the corresponding data quality, and one to represent the effect of the data mixture on fine-tuned performance.

Results: The authors compared their method to various baselines, including distributing data across domains in equal proportions and Data Mixing Optimization (DMO) , a method that automatically chooses fine-tuning mixtures based on minimizing loss. Fine-tuning on 800,000 examples, CausalMix outperformed every competing method tested on the 10 benchmarks used to select the mixtures.

Yes, but: It’s not clear how well the authors’ method extends across datasets and to other datasets. On a held-out subset of Tulu 3, CausalMix often underperformed competing methods. For example, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B on 800,000 examples from the held-out set, DMO (26.49 percent on average) outperformed CausalMix (25.04 percent on average).

Why it matters: The authors' method provides a rational approach to optimizing data mixtures rather than trial and error, and it guarantees that a good mixture will continue to apply as data or model size scales up. This makes it possible to find the best data mixture using smaller datasets and models and maintain the same proportions when scaling up without jeopardizing performance.

We’re thinking: The impact of any given training example on trained performance deepens on other examples. For instance, one example might be too hard until the model learns from another. The impact of data mixture reflects this principle. How well a model follows an instruction may depend on reasoning it learned from contemplating a math problem, and vice versa.

title: Computers Built for Local AI Apple’s Mac mini and Mac Studio have competition from Microsoft and Nvidia
excerpt: Developers have warmed to the economics and security of local models, either as an alternative or a complement to the cloud.
content:
What’s new: Apple’s upgraded Mac mini and Mac Studio desktops enable developers and AI researchers to run and fine-tune local models faster than before, offering an alternative to cloud computing for certain tasks. Nvidia’s DGX Spark series and Microsoft’s Surface Ultra laptops target a similar market: customers who want enough power to build with AI on their local machines, but in a user-friendly package.

How it works: By avoiding per-token cloud or monthly LLM subscription costs, a local setup could potentially save developers money over time, particularly [those running always-on agents]. But genuinely capable hardware is expensive: A maxed-out Mac Studio with 256GB of memory, an 80-core GPU, and 16TB of storage costs $18,299. For those with more modest local agent needs, a Mac mini starts at $899.

Performance: Apple Silicon and Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips were recently tested by an independent website, but most scores are self-reported.

Behind the news: Professionals using local AI inference are still a small market compared to the cloud, but now large enough to have genuine competition for computers designed for them at a wide range of price points. Mac desktops have sold well since the emergence of open-source personal agents, with news outlets describing weeks-long waits for Macs with more than 24GB of RAM as early as February. Nvidia’s DGX Spark laptops and desktops aim to similarly serve Windows users. For Nvidia, entering the desktop chip market ensures it can continue to sell its products to both consumer and enterprise markets, but also to increasingly blur that distinction. For Apple, it’s an alternative way to capitalize on the AI boom rather than building and hosting models, one that plays to its strengths in manufacturing high-end consumer hardware.

Why it matters: On-device AI models have several advantages over cloud-based models besides cost: more customizability, privacy, data sovereignty, potentially lower latency, and the ability to run without an internet connection. Others see cloud models and local models as complementary, designing workflows where a more powerful proprietary model solves high-level problems, then hands more mechanical work to a low-cost local model.

We’re thinking: We argued back in 2023 that strong commercial interests would increase AI usage at the edge . Not every application needs a frontier model, especially if a mid-sized model is fine-tuned to the task. But the main attraction today for local AI are privacy and data sovereignty, which is increasingly important as AI models handle more sensitive workloads. It’s useful for all of us to have a wide range of options.

title: Mistral’s Sovereign Appeal Mistral Large 4, the leading European AI model, outperforms all open models outside of China
excerpt: Mistral’s latest model is its largest and most capable, and the most powerful yet released by a European company.
content:
What’s new: Mistral announced API preview access to Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “le Chonk.” Mistral says it will release the model’s weights by the end of this month. Meanwhile, selected companies, partners, and government agencies have access to a version with limited safeguards and extra cybersecurity capabilities.

How it works: Mistral has said little about Mistral Large 4’s architecture but says it will share more when the model’s weights become available. The company says it pretrained the model from scratch and then fine-tuned it using supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning (RL).

Performance: The preview of Mistral Large 4 outscores every other model built outside China and the United States on Artificial Analysis’ popular Intelligence Index. It trails a handful of other open weights models, all from companies in China, but is ahead of all U.S.-based open models. The model preview’s strongest results come in cybersecurity tasks.

Behind the news: Mistral’s flagship models have alternated between closed and open weights and have been sometimes more and sometimes less competitive with top proprietary models. The company introduced Mistral Large , a proprietary model, in early 2024. Mistral Large 2 followed in July 2024 with weights licensed for research and non-commercial use; at the time, Mistral Large 2 was competitive with OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 3. In December 2025, Mistral released Mistral Large 3 under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, along with smaller Ministral 3 models , which the company built by repeatedly pruning and distilling the larger model.

Why it matters: The most capable open weights models on popular benchmarks are from companies based in China. Developers in the United States and Europe are trying to compete: In the U.S. Nvidia, Reflection AI, and Thinking Machines Lab, among others, have made progress, but Mistral remains the leading European lab. All of these companies pitch their models to organizations that want AI they can better control, whether via further post-training or greater trust they will be able to access the models regardless of geopolitics. Companies and governments all over the world, from South Korea to Saudi Arabia to Mexico, would prefer not to depend on either the United States or China for their access to intelligence. As Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch said earlier this year: “If you treat intelligence as electricity, then you just want to make sure that your access to intelligence cannot be throttled.”

We’re thinking: If you need AI sovereignty, and some industries and nations do, the best kind is running an open weights model on your own hardware. It doesn’t matter where a model was built (the U.S., Europe, China, or elsewhere) if your data and the model’s weights are entirely under your control.

title: Claude Fills Out Its Model Family Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 give developers fast, highly capable alternatives to Opus 5.5
excerpt: Claude Haiku, Anthropic’s fastest and least expensive model gets a long-awaited update.
content:
What’s new: Claude Haiku 5.5 replaces the year-old Claude Haiku 4.5. Independent tests show marked improvement, even with a steep price. Two weeks earlier, Anthropic launched Claude Sonnet 5.5 , which the company says is best suited to routine coding and office work, including fixing bugs and producing documents, slides, and spreadsheets. It replaces Claude Sonnet 5 at the same per-token prices.

How it works: Anthropic disclosed few details about how it built Claude Haiku 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 beyond their reasoning controls and safeguards.

Performance: Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort outperforms DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and all other “fast” models, but behind the top models. The latest Haiku version is also the fastest model Artificial Analysis has tested by tokens per second. Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max effort ranks first or second on three leaderboards from two independent testers. But at every effort setting, another model matches or outperforms Sonnet’s Artificial Analysis score at a lower cost per task.

Behind the news: Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, and Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, At launch, Opus 5.5 led Artificial Analysis and Vals AI’s overall indices. Even with the later releases of Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the top models on independent benchmark indices measuring overall intelligence.

Why it matters: Per-token prices alone don’t tell developers what a task costs. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index tests, Claude Sonnet 5.5’s cost per task varies more than eighteenfold across reasoning levels, and at max, it costs more per task than Claude Opus 5.5 set to max reasoning. On Vals AI’s tests, the cost is about two-thirds as much. Anthropic concedes Sonnet’s cost advantage over Opus is strongest at its lower reasoning levels. Claude Haiku 5.5, too, can be used as a reasoning model, but its cost advantages stand out for simpler tasks like summaries and classifications. Developers should measure each model’s cost at each relevant reasoning level on their own tasks, alongside accuracy and completion time, since each varies significantly.

We’re thinking: A higher reasoning level can change what an agent does, not just how long it reasons, and the change doesn’t always help. On FrontierCode, a test of whether an agent’s code changes are ready to merge without human edits, Anthropic says that Claude Sonnet 5.5 scores lower at max reasoning than at xhigh (46.2 percent versus 52.1 percent). Test your tasks on different effort levels to see what works best.

title: Formal Verification Meets Unverifiable Judgement Don’t Overgeneralize from Progress in Math and Code — The Hardest AI Problems Still Require More Work
excerpt: The gulf between LLM performance on verifiable tasks vs. unverifiable tasks that require judgement is larger than most people realize.
content:
The gulf between LLM performance on verifiable tasks vs. unverifiable tasks that require judgement is larger than most people realize. Verifiable tasks, like coding or solving math problems, have a right answer that can be checked automatically. Judgement tasks — like how to respond to a customer complaint, how to organize data collection for your AI project, what product feature to add, or how to form business strategies — don’t have unambiguous, ground-truth, correct answers. But they do have better and worse answers.

We have much better techniques for training AI systems to do well on verifiable tasks. As a result, progress on performing such tasks has been much faster than for judgement tasks. In the case of LLMs, RL (reinforcement learning) has been a huge driver of progress. We can set up RL gyms, or simulation environments, in which we let an LLM practice different ways to approach a task; then we automatically check which approaches are more successful (as measured by a reward function) and tune the model’s parameters to take the successful approaches more often.

For supervised learning tasks, too, verifiable tasks are easier to improve performance on. We can obtain unambiguous labels for verifiable tasks, either via automated labeling or by asking human labelers. Defining the right label for a given output in judgment tasks is much harder.

Furthermore, learning theory shows that machine learning algorithms can learn faster for tasks where it is possible to get to 0% error (called realizable tasks in the literature) than ones where the optimal error (called Bayes error) is non-zero.

It’s true that applying supervised fine-tuning to LLMs can help them learn to perform unverifiable tasks, and progress is being made here too, but data collection and eking out incremental progress is harder and slower. Intelligence is jagged, and we do have a recipe for improving AI’s capability for judgement tasks: We can collect training data and train on a specific domain, laboriously craft reward functions that capture our goals, and so on. For the subset of applications where this is valuable, businesses will invest to get this work done faster.

Society also has a long history of looking at AI’s performance on a subset of tasks and overgeneralizing its capabilities. We saw this when AI beat the human world chess champion (Deep Blue), won Jeopardy (Watson), and excelled at Go (AlphaGo). Each of these moments led to hopes about AI’s immediate applicability to other tasks that turned out to be over-optimistic. Further, we can more easily evaluate performance on verifiable tasks (since test sets are easier to create) than unverifiable ones, which creates a more optimistic impression of progress than reality can justify.

To be clear, there is a lot to be optimistic about in AI — including progress on verifiable tasks and judgement tasks! But the tremendous progress on verifiable tasks, coupled with hype around AGI and RSI, is leading people to overgeneralize to AI’s ability to do judgement tasks well. In the long term, I remain bullish about AI’s ability to do this well too, but a lot of work remains ahead.

One interesting challenge for AI Engineers is that, as verifiable tasks get automated, the need for humans to do judgement tasks — which often requires drawing context from a bewilderingly large array of raw data and identifying the pieces that critically influence a decision — remains important. As I’ve written before , I expect people to continue to have a context advantage over LLMs on many tasks for a long time.

Empowering everyone to build with AI.

Claude Haiku, Anthropic’s fastest and least expensive model gets a long-awaited update. Meanwhile, the new version of Claude Sonnet nearly matches Claude Opus 5.5 on an index of independent benchmarks, but only at a reasoning level that uses more tokens per task than any other model tested.

What’s new: Claude Haiku 5.5 replaces the year-old Claude Haiku 4.5. Independent tests show marked improvement, even with a steep price. Two weeks earlier, Anthropic launched Claude Sonnet 5.5 , which the company says is best suited to routine coding and office work, including fixing bugs and producing documents, slides, and spreadsheets. It replaces Claude Sonnet 5 at the same per-token prices.

How it works: Anthropic disclosed few details about how it built Claude Haiku 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 beyond their reasoning controls and safeguards.

Performance: Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort outperforms DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and all other “fast” models, but behind the top models. The latest Haiku version is also the fastest model Artificial Analysis has tested by tokens per second. Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max effort ranks first or second on three leaderboards from two independent testers. But at every effort setting, another model matches or outperforms Sonnet’s Artificial Analysis score at a lower cost per task.

Behind the news: Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, and Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, At launch, Opus 5.5 led Artificial Analysis and Vals AI’s overall indices. Even with the later releases of Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the top models on independent benchmark indices measuring overall intelligence.

Why it matters: Per-token prices alone don’t tell developers what a task costs. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index tests, Claude Sonnet 5.5’s cost per task varies more than eighteenfold across reasoning levels, and at max, it costs more per task than Claude Opus 5.5 set to max reasoning. On Vals AI’s tests, the cost is about two-thirds as much. Anthropic concedes Sonnet’s cost advantage over Opus is strongest at its lower reasoning levels. Claude Haiku 5.5, too, can be used as a reasoning model, but its cost advantages stand out for simpler tasks like summaries and classifications. Developers should measure each model’s cost at each relevant reasoning level on their own tasks, alongside accuracy and completion time, since each varies significantly.

We’re thinking: A higher reasoning level can change what an agent does, not just how long it reasons, and the change doesn’t always help. On FrontierCode, a test of whether an agent’s code changes are ready to merge without human edits, Anthropic says that Claude Sonnet 5.5 scores lower at max reasoning than at xhigh (46.2 percent versus 52.1 percent). Test your tasks on different effort levels to see what works best.

Mistral’s latest model is its largest and most capable, and the most powerful yet released by a European company. Its performance on independent benchmarks is comparable to GPT-6 Luna. It trails less-expensive China-based open weights models but performs better than all U.S.-based open models. It leads all models in finding and repairing a class of software vulnerabilities.

What’s new: Mistral announced API preview access to Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “le Chonk.” Mistral says it will release the model’s weights by the end of this month. Meanwhile, selected companies, partners, and government agencies have access to a version with limited safeguards and extra cybersecurity capabilities.

How it works: Mistral has said little about Mistral Large 4’s architecture but says it will share more when the model’s weights become available. The company says it pretrained the model from scratch and then fine-tuned it using supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning (RL).

Performance: The preview of Mistral Large 4 outscores every other model built outside China and the United States on Artificial Analysis’ popular Intelligence Index. It trails a handful of other open weights models, all from companies in China, but is ahead of all U.S.-based open models. The model preview’s strongest results come in cybersecurity tasks.

Behind the news: Mistral’s flagship models have alternated between closed and open weights and have been sometimes more and sometimes less competitive with top proprietary models. The company introduced Mistral Large , a proprietary model, in early 2024. Mistral Large 2 followed in July 2024 with weights licensed for research and non-commercial use; at the time, Mistral Large 2 was competitive with OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 3. In December 2025, Mistral released Mistral Large 3 under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, along with smaller Ministral 3 models , which the company built by repeatedly pruning and distilling the larger model.

Why it matters: The most capable open weights models on popular benchmarks are from companies based in China. Developers in the United States and Europe are trying to compete: In the U.S. Nvidia, Reflection AI, and Thinking Machines Lab, among others, have made progress, but Mistral remains the leading European lab. All of these companies pitch their models to organizations that want AI they can better control, whether via further post-training or greater trust they will be able to access the models regardless of geopolitics. Companies and governments all over the world, from South Korea to Saudi Arabia to Mexico, would prefer not to depend on either the United States or China for their access to intelligence. As Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch said earlier this year: “If you treat intelligence as electricity, then you just want to make sure that your access to intelligence cannot be throttled.”

We’re thinking: If you need AI sovereignty, and some industries and nations do, the best kind is running an open weights model on your own hardware. It doesn’t matter where a model was built (the U.S., Europe, China, or elsewhere) if your data and the model’s weights are entirely under your control.

Developers have warmed to the economics and security of local models, either as an alternative or a complement to the cloud. Specialized computers from Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia aim to take a bite out of the AI market with machines capable of running larger and more capable open models on-device.

What’s new: Apple’s upgraded Mac mini and Mac Studio desktops enable developers and AI researchers to run and fine-tune local models faster than before, offering an alternative to cloud computing for certain tasks. Nvidia’s DGX Spark series and Microsoft’s Surface Ultra laptops target a similar market: customers who want enough power to build with AI on their local machines, but in a user-friendly package.

How it works: By avoiding per-token cloud or monthly LLM subscription costs, a local setup could potentially save developers money over time, particularly [those running always-on agents]. But genuinely capable hardware is expensive: A maxed-out Mac Studio with 256GB of memory, an 80-core GPU, and 16TB of storage costs $18,299. For those with more modest local agent needs, a Mac mini starts at $899.

Performance: Apple Silicon and Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips were recently tested by an independent website, but most scores are self-reported.

Behind the news: Professionals using local AI inference are still a small market compared to the cloud, but now large enough to have genuine competition for computers designed for them at a wide range of price points. Mac desktops have sold well since the emergence of open-source personal agents, with news outlets describing weeks-long waits for Macs with more than 24GB of RAM as early as February. Nvidia’s DGX Spark laptops and desktops aim to similarly serve Windows users. For Nvidia, entering the desktop chip market ensures it can continue to sell its products to both consumer and enterprise markets, but also to increasingly blur that distinction. For Apple, it’s an alternative way to capitalize on the AI boom rather than building and hosting models, one that plays to its strengths in manufacturing high-end consumer hardware.

Why it matters: On-device AI models have several advantages over cloud-based models besides cost: more customizability, privacy, data sovereignty, potentially lower latency, and the ability to run without an internet connection. Others see cloud models and local models as complementary, designing workflows where a more powerful proprietary model solves high-level problems, then hands more mechanical work to a low-cost local model.

We’re thinking: We argued back in 2023 that strong commercial interests would increase AI usage at the edge . Not every application needs a frontier model, especially if a mid-sized model is fine-tuned to the task. But the main attraction today for local AI are privacy and data sovereignty, which is increasingly important as AI models handle more sensitive workloads. It’s useful for all of us to have a wide range of options.

When you’re building a fine-tuning dataset, finding a mix of subject domains that yields a high-performing model can require expensive trial and error, because fine-tuned performance also depends on the quality of the individual examples. A cause-and-effect approach aims to separate the two effects.

What's new: Researchers at Tsinghua University, Ant Group, and Renmin University of China, with Zinan Tang and Yukun Zhang as lead authors, built CausalMix , a method for choosing the share of training examples drawn from various domains regardless of their quality.

Key insight: Datasets can be analyzed according to their data mixture (the proportions of examples that represent different domains) and data quality (variations among examples in difficulty, reasoning complexity, and/or composition). Data mixture and data quality correlate, and finding their correlation in any given dataset makes it possible to differentiate their separate impacts on the performance of a model trained on the dataset. Given a dataset and a consistent training budget, to find the marginal gain of its data mixture — that is, its effect on a fine-tuned model’s performance — we can subtract the effect of data quality from the model’s performance overall. The best data mixture is the one that yields the largest marginal gain.

How it works: The authors compiled 512 subsets of 100,000 examples each drawn from the Tulu 3 dataset. Each subset contained examples for instruction following, coding, math, knowledge, and safety in different proportions. In addition, the authors measured data quality with respect to difficulty, reasoning complexity, and writing clarity as computed by OpenDataArena-Tool . They fine-tuned a separate Qwen2.5-0.5B model on each subset and recorded each fine-tuned model’s performance on 10 benchmarks. Then they trained three models, all of them ensembles of decision trees: one to estimate the portion of each Qwen2.5-0.5B’s performance attributable to data quality, one to estimate the portion of a data mixture that correlates with the corresponding data quality, and one to represent the effect of the data mixture on fine-tuned performance.

Results: The authors compared their method to various baselines, including distributing data across domains in equal proportions and Data Mixing Optimization (DMO), a method that automatically chooses fine-tuning mixtures based on minimizing loss. Fine-tuning on 800,000 examples, CausalMix outperformed every competing method tested on the 10 benchmarks used to select the mixtures.

Yes, but: It’s not clear how well the authors’ method extends across datasets and to other datasets. On a held-out subset of Tulu 3, CausalMix often underperformed competing methods. For example, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B on 800,000 examples from the held-out set, DMO (26.49 percent on average) outperformed CausalMix (25.04 percent on average).

Why it matters: The authors' method provides a rational approach to optimizing data mixtures rather than trial and error, and it guarantees that a good mixture will continue to apply as data or model size scales up. This makes it possible to find the best data mixture using smaller datasets and models and maintain the same proportions when scaling up without jeopardizing performance.

We’re thinking: The impact of any given training example on trained performance deepens on other examples. For instance, one example might be too hard until the model learns from another. The impact of data mixture reflects this principle. How well a model follows an instruction may depend on reasoning it learned from contemplating a math problem, and vice versa.

Empowering everyone to build with AI.

The best data mixture is the one that yields the largest marginal gain.

How it works: The authors compiled 512 subsets of 100,000 examples each drawn from the Tulu 3 dataset. Each subset contained examples for instruction following, coding, math, knowledge, and safety in different proportions. In addition, the authors measured data quality with respect to difficulty, reasoning complexity, and writing clarity as computed by OpenDataArena-Tool . They fine-tuned a separate Qwen2.5-0.5B model on each subset and recorded each fine-tuned model’s performance on 10 benchmarks. Then they trained three models, all of them ensembles of decision trees: one to estimate the portion of each Qwen2.5-0.5B’s performance attributable to data quality, one to estimate the portion of a data mixture that correlates with the corresponding data quality, and one to represent the effect of the data mixture on fine-tuned performance.

Results: The authors compared their method to various baselines, including distributing data across domains in equal proportions and Data Mixing Optimization (DMO), a method that automatically chooses fine-tuning mixtures based on minimizing loss. Fine-tuning on 800,000 examples, CausalMix outperformed every competing method tested on the 10 benchmarks used to select the mixtures.

Yes, but: It’s not clear how well the authors’ method extends across datasets and to other datasets. On a held-out subset of Tulu 3, CausalMix often underperformed competing methods. For example, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B on 800,000 examples from the held-out set, DMO (26.49 percent on average) outperformed CausalMix (25.04 percent on average).

Why it matters: The authors' method provides a rational approach to optimizing data mixtures rather than trial and error, and it guarantees that a good mixture will continue to apply as data or model size scales up. This makes it possible to find the best data mixture using smaller datasets and models and maintain the same proportions when scaling up without jeopardizing performance.

We’re thinking: The impact of any given training example on trained performance deepens on other examples. For instance, one example might be too hard until the model learns from another. The impact of data mixture reflects this principle. How well a model follows an instruction may depend on reasoning it learned from contemplating a math problem, and vice versa.

title: Meta’s Muse Wonder rivals top models Inside Amazon’s warehouse robotics operations
excerpt: Microsoft says it will use own chips for Copilot, MAI. Gemini 4 Argon generally available. Python 3.15 is official, Python 3.10 no longer supported.…
content:
Muse Wonder and Wonder Full bring Meta back to frontier

Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, two closed-weight models for long-running agent work such as coding, legal and finance tasks, and computer use. Both take text, image, video and audio input, return text, and have a 1 million-token context window. Muse Wonder is available through the Meta Model API at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, using an OpenAI-compatible Responses endpoint, and through the Muse Code CLI. Muse Wonder Full is limited to Muse Code plans at $50 or $200 per month. In Meta’s own benchmark table, Muse Wonder Full leads 6 of 14 rows, including DeepSWE 1.1 (79.0) and SWE-Marathon (57.5), while Claude Opus 5.5 leads ProgramBench (70.5 against 59.0), OSWorld and Terminal-Bench. Because the API matches OpenAI’s SDK format and its listed price equals Claude Opus 5.5’s, developers can trial Muse Wonder by changing a base URL and model name. Meta has not disclosed parameter counts (typical for a closed model) or a full safety report (this is less typical). ( MarkTechPost )

How Amazon is developing its huge robotics fleet

Amazon operates more than 1 million warehouse robots, mostly wheeled mobile units, and plans to grow the fleet with new robot factories in Austin, Texas, and Greenwood, Indiana. It also employs more than 1.5 million people, making it the world’s second-largest corporate employer. The newer robotic arms (Robin, Cardinal, Sparrow, Vulcan) rely on machine learning: a 2023 Amazon paper reported a 93.73 percent pick success rate for a learned model versus 92.28 percent for the best hand-coded algorithm, and Sparrow uses foundation models to handle hundreds of millions of product types. Amazon says the robots take over the riskiest tasks, but a 2025 ILR Review study of 2016-2019 data found robotic warehouses had 40 percent fewer severe injuries and 77 percent more minor strain injuries, which coauthor Brian Greenwood links to the faster work pace robots set. The arm progression shows how deployed physical AI is moving from per-product, per-robot hand-coding to general models, with small accuracy gains paying off at warehouse scale. ( Ars Technica )

Maia chips are ready for prime time, says Microsoft

Microsoft said it will scale its in-house Maia chip family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting next calendar year, making Maia the primary inference system for its own products and services. It also introduced Maia 300, which Microsoft says delivers 40 percent more tokens per watt than leading GPU-based systems. Maia 200 is already deployed in the US, Europe, and Australia, where Microsoft reports up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt in Teams and Copilot. Microsoft’s plan to run its own inference on Maia suggests it intends to rely less on GPU vendors for Copilot and Teams capacity. The post gives no benchmark methodology, comparison hardware, release date, or pricing, and does not say whether Maia will be offered to outside customers. ( Microsoft via LinkedIn )

Gemini 4 Argon available to general public, with more details

Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Argon, a sparse mixture-of-experts model with a 1M-token output limit, up from 64K on earlier Gemini models. Input and output share one 1M-token window, so a long prompt shrinks the room left for output, and long responses use a continuation protocol described in Google’s docs. Introductory API pricing is $2 input and $10 output per million tokens, rising to $4 and $20 after November 30, 2026, compared with 4/20 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 10/50 for GPT-6 Astra. In Google’s own table Argon leads on DeepSWE v1.1 (77.9%) and the Vals Index (68.9%, ranked by Vals AI), but it places last of four on FrontierSWE v2 (55.0%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (57.4%). Developers who need very long generated output, such as full code or document generation, can now get it in a single call instead of splitting work across requests. ( MarkTechPost )

How to plan for the new Python version

Python 3.15 is now officially released, and Python 3.10 is no longer supported. The release adds explicit lazy imports (PEP 810), written as lazy import json, which defer loading a module until its first use; unpacking inside comprehensions (PEP 798), such as [*L for L in lists]; and a sampling profiler, profiling.sampling (named Tachyon), in the standard library. The old tracing profiler cProfile is now profiling.tracing. Miguel Grinberg’s benchmarks of 3.15.0rc3 found speed about the same as 3.14, except the experimental just-in-time compiler, which ran a Fibonacci test 1.2x faster than the standard interpreter. For developers who support every maintained Python version, 3.10’s end of life means they can drop it and rely on 3.11 features such as tomllib, asyncio’s TaskGroup and timeout(), and new sqlite3 methods, while lazy imports offer a built-in way to cut startup cost from heavy dependencies. ( Simon Willison’s Blog )

Character.ai overspent into bankruptcy, seeks buyer

Character.ai has filed for voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy to run a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of its assets. The company cites “significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds” over the past year and does not give figures on debt, revenue, or users. It expects the sale to finish by late November or early December 2026, and says the platform will be wound down if no workable bid emerges. For now the service stays up, paid subscriptions remain active with billing unchanged, and users can delete their accounts or export their data through the app or website. Developers building with or depending on Character.ai have no guarantee of continuity until a buyer is named, so a fallback plan is prudent. ( Character.ai )

He also discussed the impact of agents on web search and analytics workloads and the necessity to optimize the software stack for these new demands. “Building data centers — which are incredibly energy- and water-efficient for the work that they do — will be a key part of this effort. Unfortunately, the anti-data center movement, which has become a rallying point for a large number of people that distrust AI technology, do not like its impact, and want to slow it down, is making it much harder to build capacity.”

title: Anthropic gives Claude Haiku a big update Microsoft-Decision-1 responds to Jev and OpenAI
excerpt: OpenAI accounting projects $50B annual revenue. Nvidia and Microsoft team up on Windows laptops. Microsoft announces AI-optimized mini-desktop. OpenAI…
content:
Claude Haiku update comes with a performance boost and price cut

Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5, its small, fast model aimed at high-volume tasks like summarization, classification, and database queries. It’s the first Haiku model with an adjustable effort setting to trade off cost against intelligence. For prompts up to 100,000 tokens, input costs drop to $0.10 per million tokens and output to $0.50 per million, versus $1.00 and $5.00 for Haiku 4.5 — roughly 90 percent cheaper for the bulk of requests, which Anthropic says covered about 90 percent of Haiku 4.5 traffic. On benchmarks, Haiku 5.5 scores far above Haiku 4.5 (for example, 72.4 percent versus 15.7 percent on the OSWorld computer-use test) and ahead of GPT-6 Luna on several tasks, though it still trails Sonnet 5.5 on complex agentic coding benchmarks like Terminal-Bench 4.0 (39.2 percent versus 70.6 percent). Anthropic also cut Sonnet 5.5’s cache-read price in half, lowering some agentic costs by about 20 percent. The company is also adding monthly API credits ($100-$500) for Max and Team subscribers plus beta SDK support for computer use and browser use. Claude Haiku 5.5 is available now on the Claude Platform, AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, giving developers a cheaper option for narrowly-scoped or subagent work that was previously too costly to run on Claude. ( Anthropic )

A speedy Jev-like decision model from Microsoft

Microsoft released Microsoft-Decision-1, a decision-scoring model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B. Given a fixed set of options (yes/no, multiple choice, ratings, or rubric grading), it returns a calibrated probability for each in a single pass through a structured API call. Microsoft says it scored highest in accuracy across a 36-benchmark comparison of nearly 150,000 questions kept blind from training, and ran 2.5 times faster than the runner-up, H2O-Lightning-4B v1.1, and 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol. The company also reports that its decision flips on 1.3 percent of input perturbations such as reordered options, that Xbox Research found it comparable to GPT-6 Sol on labeling quality while 200 times cheaper. Microsoft said it plans to rebase future versions on MAI and OpenAI models. Input costs $0.042 per million tokens and output is free, so developers can run classification, routing, and agent-gating steps on a small, low-cost model instead of a general LLM. So far, all benchmark figures come from Microsoft. ( Microsoft )

OpenAI revises revenue estimates, postpones public offering

OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate is approaching $50 billion, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg , up from over $40 billion in August but well below the nearly $70 billion figure some outlets reported last month. The Financial Times , which first reported the new estimate, said the discrepancy stems from OpenAI investors adjusting how they calculate the figure to compare more directly with rival Anthropic, including how sales through cloud providers are counted. Annualized revenue is a projection of yearly sales based on a shorter recent period, and companies don’t all calculate it the same way; Anthropic’s hit $65 billion by the end of July. Subsequent reports say that Anthropic and OpenAI still calculate cloud partner revenue differently. Currently, OpenAI is in talks to raise $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation, and has said it no longer expects to IPO this year. Public companies offer more transparency into their business, and OpenAI declining to go public this year could mean smaller AI companies may follow suit. ( Bloomberg )

Nvidia, Microsoft, partners launch AI-optimized laptops

Microsoft announced pricing and availability for the Surface Laptop Ultra, a new AI-focused laptop built on an Nvidia chip, saying it beats Apple’s MacBook Pro M5 on multiple AI model tasks. Microsoft executives claimed the device returns prompts from locally run AI models twice as fast as (and generates videos six times quicker than) a comparable Apple machine. The Ultra starts at $2,599, about $400 less than the entry-level 16-inch MacBook Pro, and ships soon. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang joined Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella to promote the chip, which also powers devices from Dell and HP. Developers weighing local inference hardware now have a Windows-based alternative to Apple-designed chips. However, Microsoft’s performance claims come from its own comparisons and haven’t been independently verified. ( Bloomberg )

Microsoft uses Nvidia chips for a Mac Studio competitor

Microsoft opened preorders for its Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, an AI-focused mini PC priced at $5,999 and shipping in November. It runs on Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform with 128GB of unified memory and a 100-watt thermal envelope. Microsoft says the machine can run local AI models exceeding 120 billion parameters for tasks like testing models, prototyping AI agents, or running coding tools on-device. As one of Microsoft’s Project Zenith devices, it ships with a developer-optimized Windows 11 Pro setup preloaded with Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub CLI, GitHub Copilot, WSL, Python, and Node. The price is higher than Nvidia’s own DGX Spark mini PC, which Microsoft attributes partly to ongoing RAM and component shortages driving PC prices up industry-wide. ( The Verge )

Watchdog calls for better guardrails on ChatGPT for Teens

The Youth AI Safety Institute designated OpenAI’s ChatGPT for Teens an “Unacceptable Risk” and called for it to be restricted to users 18 and older until its guardrails improve. The group, part of Common Sense Media, tested over 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds and found the bot failed to recommend crisis resources more than one in four times during conversations about suicide, self-harm, or disordered eating, and sent zero parent alerts for newly created accounts. Testers also said the bot disobeyed instructions, failed to switch some accounts to under-18 protections even after being told the user was 13, and had homework-answer guardrails that were easily bypassed. OpenAI disputed the methodology, saying testing may have started before parental controls were fully activated, and asked for a retest with a larger sample. Concurrently, OpenAI announced content updates to ChatGPT for Teens, including a college-application tool called College Planner and a three-year partnership with Boston Children’s Hospital’s Digital Wellness Lab. The controversy shows some of the difficulties companies face in expanding the AI market to new audiences while still offering young users highly capable services. ( The Wall Street Journal )

Last week, Andrew talked about the underestimated need for data center build-outs to support the increasing demand from agentic workflows. He also discussed the impact of agents on web search and analytics workloads and the necessity to optimize the software stack for these new demands. “Agents will drive significant transaction volume across many applications, transaction types, and sectors of the economy. Many businesses will have to redesign their systems to handle this increased scale. And to make this possible, we will need significantly more data centers that provide compute, storage, and networking.”

title: Pick the Right Tools for the Right Job Researchers designed HYSET, a technique to call collections of tools that work together
excerpt: When an LLM agent can choose among thousands of tools, picking the right ones for a given task is difficult.
content:
What’s new: Xinyi Hong at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and colleagues at Hong Kong Polytechnic University proposed HYSET , a method that constructs candidate tool sets, scores them, and chooses the best set for a given task. Previous approaches treated each tool as an independent item, rather than a set of tools suited to work well together.

Key insight: Imagine a model that receives the query, “I am flying from Chicago to Tokyo for five days next month. Find round-trip flights, book a hotel near Shinjuku, check the weather for those dates, and convert my 2,000 USD budget into yen.” How should it select the tools it needs? If it were to list the most relevant tools, the list may be topped by numerous flight APIs, while tools relevant to other parts of the task (say, a weather tool) are far down the list. The utility of a flight API, or any other tool, depends not only on its relevance to the task but also on what other tools are available.

How it works: HYSET is a small, trainable scoring model that takes as input an embedding of a query from a frozen encoder (Qwen2.5-1.5B) and outputs a list of tools for an agent . The authors trained HYSET on ToolBench, which contains roughly 14,000 tools and 200,000 instructions that describe tasks. HYSET learned, given a library of tools description of a task, to construct candidate tool sets and score each set.

Results: On ToolBench, HYSET achieved better performance than all baselines in both retrieving effective tools and completing tasks.

Why it matters: HYSET increased both (i) the completeness of retrieved tool sets, meaning the chosen set covered every tool required to complete a given task, and (ii) end-to-end task success, meaning the agent completed the task at hand with that set. paragraphs: What’s new: Xinyi Hong at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and colleagues at Hong Kong Polytechnic University proposed HYSET , a method that constructs candidate tool sets, scores them, and chooses the best set for a given task. title: Video Models Steer Robots Black Forest Labs’ Flux 3 Action applies video expertise to a World-Action Model
excerpt: Many companies that build image and video generators have pivoted to robotics, extending their expertise in world models to action.
content:
What’s new: Black Forest Labs (BFL), best known for its FLUX image generators, released FLUX 3 Action , a 7 billion-parameter model that turns camera feeds and text instructions into robot movements. It ranks first on RoboLab-120 , completing 42.9 percent of 1,200 trials. The base model and versions fine-tuned for two different robot arms (Franka and SO-101) are available on Hugging Face under BFL’s FLUX Kommunity License, which limits commercial use to companies earning less than $5 million in annual revenue.

How it works: FLUX 3 Action is a world-action model (WAM). Given camera images and a written instruction, it predicts the robot’s next moves along with what its cameras will see as a result. It also takes in the robot’s current joint positions. That differs from vision-language-action models (VLAs), such as Physical Intelligence’s π0.5 and Nvidia’s GR00T, which predict actions only.

Behind the news: Testing robots in the real world is slow, and every lab’s hardware differs, so the field leans on simulated benchmarks. Some older benchmarks have become too saturated by robots’ success to separate the best models.

Why it matters: Robot demonstration data is scarce and expensive to collect, but there’s plenty of video of the physical world. Developers of world-action models are betting that a model trained to predict video will need fewer robot examples. So far, the rankings favor that approach, but world action models tend to be larger and more demanding to run than VLAs. For developers, open weights and a fine-tuning recipe that works with a few hundred demonstrations mean a robotics research lab with a relatively low-cost arm and a powerful GPU can adapt the top-ranked model.

We’re thinking: FLUX 3 Action’s still fails more than half the time on simulated tasks. A simulated kitchen table is also tidier than a real one. We’d like to see FLUX 3 Action and its closest rivals on RoboArena next, to try their hands at more challenging robotics tasks.

title: Argon, A Low-Hallucination Model Build for Knowledge Work Google's first Gemini 4 Model, Argon, avoids hallucinations and shines at knowledge work
excerpt: Google took over half a year before it replaced its flagship AI model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview.
content:
What’s new: Google announced Gemini 4 Argon, a vision-language model trained to solve long, complex problems in software engineering, law, finance, and cybersecurity.

How it works: Google described how the model generates very long outputs and how it built safeguards around the model’s scientific and cybersecurity outputs.

Performance: Independent benchmarks rank Gemini 4 Argon well above Google’s other models and near the top of the field. It leads most tests of finance, legal, and business performance and seldom guesses wrong when it doesn’t know an answer. It still trails Anthropic’s newest models on agentic coding and Artificial Analysis’ broad index of overall intelligence.

Behind the news: Anthropic and OpenAI frequently release new models, particularly those they believe could pose a cybersecurity risk, only through gated programs (and for internal use). With Gemini 4 Argon, Google follows their example. In each case, organizations selected by the AI company get a less-restricted version first, and everyone else gets a version with more safeguards later.

Why it matters: One of Gemini 4 Argon’s strengths is long-context and high-output code migrations. Google said its agents translated C and C++ code into Rust across the company, including more than 800,000 lines from the kernel of Fuchsia, an open-source operating system that Google developed. Rust is designed to prevent many of the memory bugs that C and C++ allow. A patch fixes one vulnerability, but a rewrite in Rust addresses an entire vulnerability category. If models like Gemini 4 Argon can enable such rewrites quickly and cheaply, defenders may be able to remove specific types of vulnerabilities before attackers find them, rather than patching them piecemeal.

We’re thinking: Many models are competing to be the best software engineering assistant in the world. Gemini 4 Argon may not be the most powerful coder, but Vals AI’s index shows its strengths in fields like finance, taxes, and law. Gemini 4 Argon is also the frontier model most likely to admit it doesn’t know the answer to a factual question rather than guess wrong. In a financial analysis or legal brief, a confident incorrect answer may slide past a reviewer, while a refusal is obvious and can be passed to a person or another model — assuming applications using it have a plan for questions the model won’t answer.

title: Sol Nearly Eclipses Astra OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol is DevDay’s star, joined by Dots and new ChatGPT integrations
excerpt: OpenAI’s latest mid-tier model lands within a point of its flagship at less than a quarter of the cost per task on Artificial Analysis'...
content:
What’s new: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol on September 29 at its annual DevDay developer conference. The company says the model nearly matches GPT-6 Astra on agentic coding, computer use, and professional work at one-fifth of Astra's standard per-token prices. At the same event, OpenAI introduced Dots — always-on personal agents that run on GPT-6 Astra.

How it works: OpenAI disclosed little about GPT-6.1 Sol’s architecture or training beyond saying that it uses the same types of data and training as GPT-6 Astra.

Results: Artificial Analysis’ independent tests largely back OpenAI’s claim that GPT-6.1 Sol rivals Astra, though Anthropic and Google models lead on some measures.

Behind the news: OpenAI called DevDay 2026 its biggest yet, with more than 20 announcements, and cited 1.2 billion weekly users.

What didn’t ship: GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released September 3, won’t get a matching upgrade for now. The day before DevDay, The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI had canceled the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra. In internal tests, the model showed more deception than GPT-6 Astra, including inaccurate accounts of which actions it had taken, and it sometimes pressed ahead with tasks without asking permission. OpenAI hopes to reuse GPT-6.1 Astra’s base model for reinforcement learning of future GPT-6 models.

Why it matters: Agents, which loop through many steps, reread long contexts, and work without supervision, stand to benefit most from GPT-6.1 Sol’s performance-to-price ratio and model guardrails. But that puts much of the weight on the guardrails around them. Given all this, it’s somewhat surprising that Dots don’t run on GPT-6.1 Sol, but the somewhat older and more expensive GPT-6 Astra.

We’re thinking: OpenAI says it held back GPT-6.1 Astra because the model didn’t meet its own security bar, even though that meant scrapping an October launch. Artificial Analysis published its own measurements of GPT-6.1 Sol the day it debuted. But Dots, which connect to users’ apps and act around the clock, have no comparable outside yardstick yet. We'd like to see independent testers put Dots and their agentic rivals through more rigorous tests of their security and capabilities like those that appeared to have stopped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra.
